content: The implementation of a nurse-led model for initiating treatment in patients with hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, including those with cirrhosis, involved a two-day training program for nurses. To accelerate the initiation of direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapy for HCV viremic patients, nurses conducted pre-treatment assessments. Patients without additional complications received follow-up care at local health centers under the supervision of trained nurses. However, patients with decompensated cirrhosis, prior DAA treatment, hepatitis B virus (HBV) co-infection, or other comorbidities requiring closer observation continued to receive care from general physicians at referral hospitals. Eligible patients were prescribed a daily oral regimen of sofosbuvir (400 mg) and daclatasvir (60 mg) for 12 weeks. For those with decompensated cirrhosis or prior DAA treatment, the regimen was extended to 24 weeks. Between June 1, 2020, and September 30, 2020, 10,960 residents were screened for HCV, with 43% identified through active case finding and 57% through passive case finding. This screening effort covered approximately 8% of the estimated 136,571 adults in the operational health district of Moung Russei. Among the 920 individuals who tested positive for HCV antibodies, 98% underwent HCV RNA viral load testing, and 61% (547 patients) were confirmed to be viremic, with a median age of 58 years. Of the 547 viremic patients, 97% were successfully linked to treatment and follow-up care. A total of 204 patients (38%) were referred to referral hospitals for DAA initiation, while 329 patients (62%) began treatment at local health centers. The median time from HCV viral load testing to treatment initiation at health centers was eight days. Among those treated, 94% achieved sustained virologic response at 12 weeks (SVR12), with only five cases of treatment failure. The pilot project demonstrated that a simplified, decentralized, nurse-led care model for HCV management can be effectively integrated into rural public health systems in low-income settings. This approach maintained high patient retention, treatment efficacy, and safety. By utilizing accessible primary health centers and non-specialist clinical staff, the program optimized limited resources and expanded the capacity to test and treat individuals with HCV infection. The success of Malaysia’s HCV program, which progressively decentralized HCV screening and treatment, was attributed to a multi-faceted strategy. This included strong government commitment, a five-year national strategic plan launched in 2019, and evidence-based clinical practice guidelines. Improved access to DAAs was achieved through a compulsory license for sofosbuvir, reducing treatment costs to less than USD $300 per patient in public health facilities. The care model shifted from hospital-based to community-based services, initially piloted in 25 primary health care centers and later expanded to 287 centers. Capacity building for healthcare workers was supported through training sessions and periodic workshops to address clinical and service delivery challenges. By August 2021, despite the COVID-19 pandemic, over 11,000 HCV patients had been treated with DAAs. In Georgia, the world’s first national HCV elimination program was launched in 2015. By 2021, 3 million individuals had been screened, and 76,000 of the estimated 150,000 individuals with chronic HCV infection had been treated. The program emphasized simplified diagnostic pathways, decentralized care, and integration with primary and harm reduction services. Reflex testing for HCV RNA was introduced in 2017, significantly improving diagnostic efficiency. Integration with harm reduction services increased screening rates among people who inject drugs, with high rates of treatment initiation and cure. Task-sharing initiatives allowed primary care physicians to manage HCV treatment, further decentralizing care. Peer-based models, such as those implemented in Georgia, Kenya, and Vietnam, demonstrated the effectiveness of integrating HCV care into harm reduction services. These models achieved high retention and cure rates, with peer navigators playing a critical role in guiding patients through the care continuum. In Myanmar, HCV treatment was integrated into existing HIV-focused harm reduction programs. Peer navigators facilitated awareness, testing, and adherence, while minimal additional resources were required to incorporate HCV care. Despite challenging humanitarian conditions, the program achieved cure rates exceeding 86% and treated the majority of eligible patients within two years. National planning for HCV elimination, as guided by the World Health Organization (WHO), emphasizes evidence-based decision-making, simplified algorithms for testing and treatment, and differentiated care approaches tailored to individual needs. Integration of HCV services with existing health systems, including HIV and harm reduction programs, has proven effective in increasing access and improving outcomes. Simplified diagnostic and treatment pathways, combined with efficient procurement and supply management, are essential for scaling up HCV care and achieving elimination goals.
